\chapter{Ne and Dui}
\label{ch:zh-ne-dui}
\hlchaptermodality{26}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hand a question back with \zh{呢}, agree with what somebody has said, and ask whether something is right.}

Thirteen strokes make the first two-sided exchange in this book: \zh{吗} could ask, and until now nothing could hand the question back or agree with the answer.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ne]{\zh{呢} — \zh{吗}'s shape, a different sound}

\label{lesson:ZH-W26-ne}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, and its first character is one you half know.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ kàn le shū} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{le} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hǎo bu hǎo} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zì — hànzì — hànyǔ — zhōngwén — zhōngguó} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dà} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the same mouth, a different right half}
\begin{quote}
\zh{呢}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Eight strokes}, and the first three are ones you have written since the fourth chapter.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{口}'s \textbf{shù} down the left side
  \item \zh{口}'s \textbf{héngzhé} across the top and down the right
  \item \zh{口}'s \textbf{héng} closing the floor
\end{enumerate}

That is the same \zh{口}, in the same order, set small and high in the upper-left third of the square — \textbf{exactly where \zh{吗} puts it.} Finish it before the right half starts.

Then \zh{尼} \emph{ní}, which supplies only the sound:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{héngzhé} across the top of the right half and down at its right
  \item the \textbf{héng} beneath it
  \item the long \textbf{piě}, falling from the top all the way down to the lower left, past the bottom of \zh{口}
  \item a short \textbf{piě} inside, falling left
  \item the \textbf{shùwāngōu}, turning along the base and finishing to the right
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Stroke 6 is the one that carries the character.} It starts high and reaches the lower-left corner, and everything after it tucks inside.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{口} — then \zh{呢}, mouth first
  \item \emph{Cover:} write \zh{吗} and \zh{呢} side by side and compare the left halves
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which three strokes open \zh{呢}? (\textbf{\zh{口}'s} — vertical, turn, floor.) Which other character starts the same way? (\textbf{\zh{吗}}.) Which stroke is the long one? (\textbf{The sixth}, falling to the lower left.)

Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%91\%A2.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{呢}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ne]{\zh{呢} — and you?}

\label{lesson:ZH-C26-ne}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and the character is under your pen.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ne} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{le} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ shì} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shì ma} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zì — hànzì — hànyǔ — zhōngwén — zhōngguó} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dà} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: put \zh{呢} after a noun and it asks the last question again}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{呢}} \emph{ne} — toneless, placed after a noun or a pronoun. It repeats whatever question was on the table, about this one instead.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{\zh{你是学生吗}} — Are you a student? — \textbf{\zh{我是学生你呢}} \emph{nǐ ne} — I'm a student. \textbf{And you?}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\zh{你呢}} is two syllables and a complete turn. Nothing has to be repeated: \zh{呢} carries the whole of the previous question with it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我是中国人你呢}} \textbf{\zh{我有一个名字你呢}} \textbf{\zh{我看了书你呢}}
\end{quote}

Every one of those means something different, and \zh{呢} is the same in all of them, because the question it asks is whichever one was already on the table.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — the second particle, and the pair}]
Keep \zh{吗} and \zh{呢} apart by what comes before them:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\zh{吗}} & after a \textbf{whole statement} & \zh{你是学生吗} — a yes-or-no question \\
\textbf{\zh{呢}} & after a \textbf{noun} & \zh{你呢} — the last question, asked again \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

They cannot be swapped. \emph{\zh{你吗}} is not a question and \emph{\zh{你是学生呢}} is not the question you meant.

\zh{呢} is the second of Mandarin's particles this book has taught, and the third toneless word after \zh{吗} and \zh{的}. \textbf{A Mandarin sentence's grammar lives in words like these} — small, unstressed, unchanging, and placed rather than inflected. That is what the reader is learning each time one arrives.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{我是学生你呢}
  \item \zh{我是中国人你呢}
  \item \zh{你是学生吗} — \zh{你呢} — hear the difference
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \zh{呢} do? (\textbf{Asks the last question again, about somebody else}.) What comes before it? (\textbf{A noun} — \zh{你呢}.) And what comes before \zh{吗}? (\textbf{A whole statement}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[duì]{\zh{对} — five strokes, and a hand on the left}

\label{lesson:ZH-W26-dui}



\begin{quote}
Two lessons in, and this one is short.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ne} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ shì dàxuéshēng le} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shū} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shì ma} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zì — hànzì — hànyǔ — zhōngwén — zhōngguó} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{rén — nǚ — érzi — nǚ'ér — jiā — jiārén} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — a hand, and a thumb's width}
\begin{quote}
\zh{对}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Five strokes.} Two on the left, three on the right.

The left half is \zh{又}, an old picture of a hand:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{héngpiě} — a short flat start that turns and falls to the lower left, one stroke, no lift
  \item the \textbf{nà}, crossing it and falling to the lower right
\end{enumerate}

The right half is \zh{寸}:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{héng} across the right half
  \item the long \textbf{shùgōu} down through it, hooking left at the foot
  \item the \textbf{diǎn} dot, placed last, to the left of the hook
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{The dot is the final stroke} — the same rule \zh{的} followed. And the left half is finished before the right begins, as always.

Hold on to strokes 1 and 2. That \zh{又} opens \textbf{\zh{欢}} two chapters from now, and you will not have to learn it twice.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{对} — \zh{又}'s two, then \zh{寸}'s three, dot last
  \item \emph{Cover:} write it again from memory
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes does \zh{对} have? (\textbf{Five}.) Which stroke is the dot? (\textbf{The last}.) And which later character shares its left half? (\textbf{\zh{欢}}.)

Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%AF\%B9.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{对}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[duì]{\zh{对} — right, and the sound of agreeing}

\label{lesson:ZH-C26-dui}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and this word does two jobs.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{duì} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{le} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Zhōngguó rén} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nǐ hǎo ma} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{jiārén} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{对}} \emph{duì} is \textbf{fourth tone} — the sharp fall, the same shape as \zh{四}, \zh{六} and \zh{个}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{对}} — Right. Correct. \textbf{\zh{不对}} \emph{bú duì} — Wrong. Not right. \textbf{\zh{对不对}} \emph{duì bu duì} — Right or not?
\end{quote}

That last one is a shape you already own. The asking chapter taught \textbf{\zh{好不好}}, the verb-not-verb question, and \textbf{\zh{对不对}} is the same pattern on a new word — no new grammar at all, one new syllable.

And the \zh{不} in front of \zh{对} rises: \emph{bú duì}, not \emph{bù duì}. That is the \zh{不} sandhi the \zh{是} chapter taught on \zh{不是}, working exactly as it did there, because \zh{对} is fourth tone too.
\end{sounds}

\begin{culture}
On its own, \textbf{\zh{对}} is what a Mandarin speaker says while somebody else is talking to show they are following and they agree. English uses \emph{right}, \emph{yeah}, \emph{mm}; Mandarin uses \textbf{\zh{对}}, often doubled — \textbf{\zh{对对}}

Until this line, this book had no backchannel at all. You could greet, ask, count and name, and while somebody spoke to you there was nothing to say. That is not a small gap: a listener who makes no sound at all reads, in Mandarin as in English, as a listener who has not understood.

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{\zh{你是中国人吗}} — \textbf{\zh{对}}
\end{quote}

Two syllables, and a whole exchange finished.

Careful with one thing. \textbf{\zh{对}} agrees with a \textbf{statement}. It is not a general \emph{yes}: asked a question with a verb in it, a Mandarin speaker answers by repeating the verb — \textbf{\zh{是}} for a \zh{是} question, \textbf{\zh{有}} for a \zh{有} question. \zh{对} is for agreeing that what was said is so.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{对} \zh{不对} \zh{对不对}
  \item \zh{你是中国人吗} — \zh{对}
  \item \zh{对对}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \zh{对} mean? (\textbf{Right, correct}.) What does it do on its own in a conversation? (\textbf{Shows you are following and agree}.) And how is \zh{不对} said? (\emph{\textbf{Bú duì}} — \zh{不} rises before a fourth tone.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\zh{你呢} — \zh{对不对}}

\label{lesson:ZH-C26-practice}



\begin{quote}
The chapter closes with an exchange rather than a word.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{duì} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ kàn le shū} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Zhōngguó rén — shū — kàn} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nǐ hǎo ma} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yán} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — a turn each way}]
Two characters, thirteen strokes, and here is what they buy — a conversation that goes both ways:

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{\zh{你是学生吗}} — \textbf{\zh{对你呢}} — \textbf{\zh{我是大学生了}} — \textbf{\zh{对对}}
\end{quote}

Every line of that is short, and none of it was sayable before this chapter. \zh{吗} could ask; nothing could hand the question back, and nothing could agree.

\textbf{\zh{呢}} after a noun asks the last question again. \textbf{\zh{对}} agrees with a statement. \textbf{\zh{吗}} after a whole statement asks a yes-or-no question. Three particles, three slots, and not one of them changes shape.

\textbf{Listen.} \emph{Nǐ shì xuésheng ma? — Duì. Nǐ ne?}

\textbf{Speak.} Answer, then hand it back with \zh{你呢}.

\textbf{Read.} \zh{你是学生吗} — \zh{对} — \zh{你呢}

\textbf{Write.} \zh{呢} — \zh{口} first. \zh{对} — \zh{又} first, dot last.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{你是学生吗} — \zh{对你呢}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{对不对} — \zh{对}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{呢} \zh{对}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which particle hands the question back? (\textbf{\zh{呢}}, after a noun.) Which word agrees with a statement? (\textbf{\zh{对}}.) And which one turns a statement into a question? (\textbf{\zh{吗}}, at the end.)
\end{tcolorbox}
